answer.label: Attributed in a specific book citation to
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is credited to Simone de Beauvoir’s All Said and Done, page 16, by Wikiquote. It is also quoted with that book title in Canadian government symposium proceedings; the original page has not been inspected here.

source.heading: The source
trail: Wikiquote’s entry ↗ supplies the book and page citation.
The Canadian proceedings ↗ repeat the sentence in a discussion of information about women’s lives. The bibliographic record ↗ distinguishes the English translation from the French original.
source.rightsNote: The English wording belongs to a modern translated memoir. It is treated as copyrighted; the 1972 French date is not used as a date for the English translation.

author.name: Simone de Beauvoir
author.heading: About Simone de Beauvoir
author.bio: Simone de Beauvoir explored freedom, responsibility and women’s situation through philosophy, fiction and memoir. The Second Sex became a foundational feminist work; her four-volume autobiography concludes with All Said and Done.

cite.sourceCitation: Beauvoir, Simone de. All Said and Done, p. 16, as cited by Wikiquote. English translation metadata: Patrick O’Brian, 1974; French original Tout compte fait, 1972. Original page not inspected.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘I tore myself away from the safe comfort of certainties through my love for truth — and truth rewarded me’?” Last verified 9 Nov 2026.

copyAttribution: Attributed to Simone de Beauvoir, All Said and Done, p. 16; specific secondary citation, original page not inspected. English translation by Patrick O’Brian (1974).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is cited to Beauvoir’s final autobiographical volume, a retrospective account of her thinking and life. Its later use in a symposium on gender statistics turns the contrast between certainty and truth into a call to improve the evidence available about women’s lives.
